content: The Ottawa ankle rules are a set of clinical guidelines designed to assist physicians in determining whether a patient presenting with foot or ankle pain requires radiographic imaging (X-rays) to evaluate for a potential bone fracture. Prior to the development of these rules, most patients with ankle injuries underwent X-rays, despite the fact that only approximately 15% of these imaging studies revealed fractures. The majority of cases involved sprains or other soft tissue injuries. This practice led to a significant number of unnecessary X-rays, which were not only costly and time-consuming but also posed potential health risks due to radiation exposure. The Ottawa ankle rules were developed by a team of emergency medicine specialists in Ottawa, Canada. The guidelines were named after the city where they were created, following a convention similar to that of the Glasgow Coma Scale, which is also named after its city of origin. The rules have since become widely recognized and adopted in clinical practice. According to the Ottawa ankle rules, X-rays are only indicated if there is bony pain in the malleolar or midfoot region, accompanied by at least one of the following criteria: Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior edge of the tibia or the tip of the medial malleolus. Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior edge of the fibula or the tip of the lateral malleolus. Bone tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal (specific to foot injuries). Bone tenderness at the navicular bone (specific to foot injuries). Inability to bear weight both immediately after the injury and in the emergency department for four consecutive steps. Certain populations are excluded from the application of these rules, including children under the age of 18, pregnant women, and individuals with impaired ability to cooperate with the assessment (e.g., due to head injury or intoxication). The utility of the Ottawa ankle rules has been extensively validated. Initial research demonstrated that the rules had a sensitivity of 100%, meaning they were highly effective at identifying fractures when present, and they reduced the number of unnecessary ankle X-rays by approximately 35%. A subsequent larger trial confirmed these findings, and a multi-center study later explored the feasibility of implementing the rules on a broader scale. Although the original Ottawa ankle rules were specifically developed for ankle and foot injuries, similar clinical decision-making guidelines have since been adapted for other joints, such as the knee, to optimize the use of imaging and improve patient care.
